nameStory: The hairy lip fern gets its name from the soft, sparse hairs that cover its fronds, giving them a slightly fuzzy texture when you run your fingers along them. Unlike many other ferns that have scales on their leaves, this species relies on its fine hairs for protection, making it quite distinctive to the touch.
description: Hairy lip fern is a medium-sized fern that forms compact clumps in rocky, dry places where most other ferns wouldn't dare to grow. Its fronds are twice-divided, creating a delicate, lacy appearance with narrow, oblong segments that fan out beautifully. The entire plant has a soft, slightly fuzzy texture due to the fine hairs covering the leaves, and it's perfectly adapted to survive in surprisingly dry conditions for a fern.

idTips.label: Fronds
idTips.description: Twice-divided fronds with narrow, lance-shaped or oblong segments that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch due to sparse hairs covering the surface

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms compact, clumping colonies rather than spreading widely, with multiple fronds emerging from a central point

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Grows in surprisingly dry, rocky locations with shallow soil where most other ferns cannot survive

idTips.label: Stipe
idTips.description: Dark, wiry stems that feel firm and somewhat brittle, supporting the delicate fronds above rocky crevices

idTips.label: Sori
idTips.description: Spore cases are protected by the rolled-under margins of the leaf segments, creating a distinctive 'lip' appearance

habitat: Hairy lip fern thrives in dry, rocky habitats with shallow soil - exactly the opposite of where you'd expect to find most ferns. Look for it tucked into rock crevices, on cliff faces, or in rocky slopes where the soil drains quickly and stays relatively dry. It's particularly fond of limestone and other alkaline rock formations.

seasonality.spring: New fiddleheads emerge from rocky crevices, unfurling into fresh green fronds with their characteristic soft, hairy texture becoming apparent as they mature.
seasonality.summer: Fronds reach full size and develop spore cases along the rolled margins. The hairs are most noticeable during warm, dry weather when you can easily feel their soft texture.
seasonality.fall: Fronds begin to brown and release spores. The plant starts to go dormant as temperatures drop, with fronds gradually withering.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground fronds die back completely, leaving only the underground portions alive to survive the cold season in rocky crevices.

funFact: This fern is essentially a desert survivor hiding in New England - it can actually photosynthesize and stay green even when it loses up to 95% of its water content, then bounce back to life with the next rainfall like a botanical resurrection!
confusionNotes: With only one recorded observation in New England, you're more likely to mistake a dried-up common fern for hairy lip fern than to actually find one. The key difference is the persistently hairy texture and the extremely dry, rocky habitat - if you're in a moist, woodsy spot, it's definitely not hairy lip fern.
contextualKnowledge: Until 2013, this species was classified in the genus Cheilanthes and called Cheilanthes lanosa, so you might still see it listed under that name in older field guides. The scientific name was changed when botanists recognized that the lip ferns deserved their own separate genus, Myriopteris.
compareHints: Since hairy lip fern is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it to other drought-tolerant ferns in the brake family. Unlike the similar-looking cliff brake ferns, hairy lip fern has obvious soft hairs on its fronds rather than a waxy or scaly coating, and its segments are more oblong rather than narrow and linear.
